hook: In 2026 creative strategists should steal from screenwriters
body: The unlock: AI drama ads are trending and everyone will copy the same 5 stories -- so stop swiping ads and start swiping screenplays. A series holds you for 8 episodes; screenwriters are elite at emotion. The example: a crime-show scene of a marriage losing attraction, engineered to be relatable and intense -- then bridge it to a product (libido supp, hormone support, couples angle). Before the next AI drama ad, open Netflix, not the ad library.
idea: Swipe screenplays, not ads: screenwriters' emotional engineering is the raw material; the product bridge comes after.

idea: Entertaining is not enough: AI drama ads must be built with conversion intention.

body: The conversion recipe: take your winning ad and turn it into a 2-3 minute storytelling ad. Use engaging stories with catchy hooks like Resilia's (cheating husband, cheating wife, wife compared to another girl). People like drama ads because they're entertaining, especially with multiple cuts keeping them hooked. The transcript is the Linda/Graham/Carol scene: a wife mistaken for the caterers, the garden-centre comparison, the slimming-club history, the transformation reveal.
idea: Turn your winning ad into a 2-3 minute story: the winner's message plus drama's retention equals the easiest conversion opportunity.
formatting: X post with transcript; no video in the file.
why_it_works: The winner's message is pre-validated; drama is just the retention wrapper that lets it run long.
what_to_steal: Louise Carter's drama lane: take the best-performing UGC winner and expand it into a 2-3 minute story with the jewelry as the transformation.

hook: AI UGC is already dominating every major ad platform.
body: The strategist takeaway: women consume advertising differently -- stories, drama, characters, relationships, tension, resolution. Micro-dramas prove it. The traditional UGC flywheel (hook -> problem -> solution -> CTA) is predictable; consumers know the pattern. The next edge: make something people would watch with nothing being sold, then map the product into the entertainment. Example: a shopping-channel-inspired mascara ad.
idea: Ads become entertainment, entertainment becomes distribution: the product gets written directly into the story.
sequencing: The takeaway: women consume ads differently
formatting: X essay post with a 141s video (video.twimg.com, 1080x1920) and transcript.
why_it_works: The gendered consumption insight plus the pattern-recognition critique makes entertainment-first feel inevitable.
what_to_steal: Louise Carter's audience is women: build story-first AI drama with the jewelry written into the plot, not bolted on as a CTA.

hook: The hardest part about making AI ads for GLP brands isn't the AI.
body: The scrutiny thesis: GLP is one of the most scrutinized ad categories -- every claim gets checked, every visual questioned. You can't hide bad creative behind novelty. If you can make great ads under that scrutiny, you can make them anywhere. The transcript is the Maximus ad: for men, losing weight was never supposed to mean becoming less of yourself -- perform, run harder, lift heavier.
idea: Scrutinized categories are the proving ground: cinematic, realistic AI ads that survive claim-checking work anywhere.
formatting: X post with a 61s video (video.twimg.com, 1080x1920) and transcript.
what_to_steal: Hold Louise Carter's AI drama to the scrutiny standard: every jewelry claim (waterproof, warranty) must survive checking, no novelty-hiding.

body: The show thesis: women want characters, drama, relationships, tension, payoff -- not an ad ambush 8 seconds into the scroll. Build the entertainment first, then work the product in slowly. Entertainment value is the currency you spend to earn product attention; if the story is good, people sit through the product education. The account signals: cheap CPMs, strong CPAs, scale. Stop interrupting the show; make the ad the show. The transcript is an office-drama scene.
idea: Make the ad the show: entertainment first, product woven in -- entertainment value is the currency that buys product attention.
sequencing: The closer: stop interrupting, make the show
formatting: X essay post with a 420s video (video.twimg.com, 1080x1920) and transcript.
why_it_works: The currency metaphor makes the entertainment investment feel like media buying, not art.
what_to_steal: Louise Carter's drama KPI: entertainment first, product education second -- and watch for the cheap-CPM/strong-CPA signal that the balance is right.

hook: Koriderm is absolutely CRUSHING with these DRAMA ads rn.
body: The 6-step AI drama tutorial: (1) create the drama story -- never show the product in the first 3 seconds; story around the problem (stain remover example: coffee on the wedding dress, mother panicking, groom waiting); (2) write the full script with ChatGPT/Claude (90 seconds, shocking start, 2-3 characters, tension, problem worsens, product as solution, 5-8 second scenes); (3) create characters with GPT Image/Nano Banana (reference images for consistency); (4) animate scenes with Seedance/Kling/Veo, 5-8s each with dialogue/action/emotion; (5) reveal the product with a real image, solve the character's problem honestly; (6) assemble in CapCut (captions, music, SFX), fast opening, tension middle, satisfying payoff, 9:16, test openings.
idea: The 6-step mini-movie pipeline: shocking story first, product as the solution later -- attention hacking via narrative.
sequencing: Step 1: drama story, no product in first 3s
formatting: X tutorial post with a 60s video and photo.
why_it_works: Each step is a concrete operation with a tool attached; the wedding-dress example makes the abstract instantly visual.
what_to_steal: The 6-step pipeline as Louise Carter's drama SOP, with the wedding-dress stakes translated: green skin discovered at the wedding, Louise Carter as the solution.

hook: i think the best drama ads are the ones where people can actually see themselves in the scenario.
body: The aspiration thesis: the best drama ads let viewers experience a version of themselves they secretly want to become -- a lifestyle, a personality trait, a behavior. Don't copy whatever brand is printing; understand your demographic, what they aspire to, how they want to be perceived. Come up with the concept yourself before briefing AI; the idea comes from you, AI brings it to life.
idea: Aspirational identification is the drama mechanism: let the viewer live the version of herself she secretly wants to become.
why_it_works: Aspirational identification is the oldest persuasion lever, restated for AI drama.
what_to_steal: Louise Carter's drama concepts should start from the customer's aspirational self (effortless, radiant, noticed) -- and the human writes the concept before AI touches the script.
